questions.question: The server answers this call with HTTP 500. What happens at the call site?
options: It throws `HttpException` whose `code()` is 500
It returns `null` because the body couldn't be parsed
It returns a `User` with default field values
It throws `IOException` because the request failed
questions.explanation: When a suspend Retrofit method returns the body type `T` directly, any non-2xx response throws `retrofit2.HttpException`. `IOException` is for transport failures (no connection, timeout), not for a server that did answer.

questions.question: A Retrofit `suspend` function can be called directly from `viewModelScope.launch` (which runs on the main thread) without wrapping it in `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)`.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Retrofit's suspend support enqueues the call on OkHttp's own dispatcher threads and resumes the coroutine with the result, so the call is main-safe. Adding `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` is harmless but unnecessary.

questions.question: A retry helper computes its delays like this. What does it print?
questions.explanation: Each delay is recorded before doubling, so the list starts at 100. The fourth doubling would give 800, but `coerceAtMost(500)` caps it at 500. Capping exponential backoff stops retry waits from growing without limit.

questions.question: Every repository in the app builds its own `OkHttpClient()` (some even build one per request). What is the main problem?
options: Each client has its own connection pool, threads and cache, so none are reused
OkHttp throws an exception when more than one client exists in a process
Interceptors are registered globally, so each new client adds them a second time
Nothing, because `OkHttpClient()` returns an internal singleton
questions.explanation: OkHttp performs best with a single shared client: connection pool, dispatcher and cache all belong to the instance. For a variant (say, a longer timeout), call `sharedClient.newBuilder()`, which reuses the same pool and dispatcher. Multiple clients are legal, just wasteful.

questions.question: An app targeting a recent SDK calls `http://api.example.com` and fails with "CLEARTEXT communication to api.example.com not permitted by network security policy". Which changes make the request succeed?
options: Switch the URL to `https://`
Add a network security config `domain-config` with `cleartextTrafficPermitted="true"` for that domain
Add the `INTERNET` permission to the manifest
Increase OkHttp's `connectTimeout`
questions.explanation: Since API 28, cleartext HTTP is blocked by default. HTTPS is the right fix, and a domain-scoped network security config exception also works (for example for a local dev server). The error isn't about permissions or timeouts: a missing `INTERNET` permission fails differently.

questions.question: The backend adds a new `avatar` field to the user JSON. The app decodes with a default `Json` instance. What happens?
options: Decoding throws a `SerializationException` for the unknown key
The extra field is silently ignored, as with Gson and Moshi
Decoding succeeds and `avatar` is kept in a hidden extras map
The code stops compiling until `avatar` is added to the class
questions.explanation: kotlinx.serialization is strict by default and rejects keys the class doesn't declare. Gson and Moshi ignore unknown fields, which is why people expect that here. For network models, `ignoreUnknownKeys = true` keeps old app versions working when the server adds fields.

questions.question: Leaving `HttpLoggingInterceptor` at `Level.BODY` in release builds is harmless, because only your app can read its own logs.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Logs show up in `adb logcat` and in bug reports, so `BODY` leaks tokens and personal data. It also buffers every body, which costs memory and speed. Enable it only in debug builds (e.g. `if (BuildConfig.DEBUG)`), use `Level.NONE`/`BASIC` otherwise, and `redactHeader("Authorization")`.

questions.question: The server returns 404 with a JSON error body. What do you get?
options: No exception: `isSuccessful` is false and the error JSON is in `errorBody()`
It throws `HttpException` for the 404, the same as a method returning `User` does
`body()` holds the error JSON parsed into a `User`
`isSuccessful` is true because the server sent a response
questions.explanation: Wrapping the type in `Response<T>` means Retrofit doesn't throw for non-2xx statuses. You check `code()`/`isSuccessful` yourself and read the error with `errorBody()` (`body()` is null), which can be read only once. Network failures still throw `IOException`.

questions.question: Gson (via `GsonConverterFactory`) parses `{}` into this Kotlin class. Which statements are true?
questions.code:
data class User(val name: String, val age: Int = 18)

val u = gson.fromJson("{}", User::class.java)
options: `u.name` is null at runtime despite its non-null `String` type, so a later use can throw NPE
`u.age` is 0, not 18
Gson throws `JsonSyntaxException` because `name` is missing
Gson calls the primary constructor, so `age` is 18
questions.explanation: The class has no no-arg constructor, so Gson allocates the object with `Unsafe` and skips the Kotlin constructor completely. That bypasses both the null checks and the default values. Moshi's Kotlin support and kotlinx.serialization respect nullability and defaults.

questions.question: Decoding `{"role": null}` into `@Serializable data class Member(val role: String = "user")` with a default `Json` fails, but with `Json { coerceInputValues = true }` it gives `Member(role = "user")`.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A default value is used only when a key is missing, not when it is an explicit `null`. So a null for a non-null property is an error by default. `coerceInputValues = true` replaces such nulls (and unknown enum values) with the property's default.

questions.question: This interceptor is supposed to add a bearer token. What does it actually do?
options: It sends the original request without the header, because the rebuilt request is discarded
It crashes, because inside an interceptor `header()` must be `addHeader()` to modify a request
It sends the `Authorization` header twice
It adds the header correctly
questions.explanation: `Request` is immutable: `newBuilder().build()` returns a new object, and here that object is thrown away. The fix is `chain.proceed(request.newBuilder().header("Authorization", "Bearer $token").build())`. `header()` replaces any existing value and `addHeader()` appends, and both are valid.

questions.question: A repository maps exceptions to domain errors. What does this print?
options: Network, Server, Client, Unknown
Unknown, Server, Client, Unknown
Network, Server, Unauthorized, Unknown
Network, Server, Client, Network
questions.explanation: `SocketTimeoutException` extends `IOException`, so it maps to `Network`. 503 is in `500..599` and 404 falls to `else`, giving `Client`. `IllegalStateException` matches neither type. Retrofit splits errors the same way: `HttpException` means the server answered with an error, `IOException` means the transport failed.

questions.question: The client uses OkHttp's defaults (connect/read/write 10 s, no call timeout). A download trickles one byte every 5 seconds for 10 minutes. What happens?
options: It finishes after about 10 minutes; no single read waits more than 10 s
It fails after 10 s with a read timeout, since the transfer runs past `readTimeout`
It fails after 10 s with a connect timeout
It fails after 30 s, the sum of the three timeouts
questions.explanation: `readTimeout` limits how long one read can wait between bytes, not how long the whole transfer takes. Only `callTimeout` covers the entire call (DNS, connect, write, server time, read), and it is disabled by default.

questions.question: A repository wraps `api.me()` (a suspend function returning `User`) in a try/catch. Which statements are correct?
options: `IOException` (e.g. `UnknownHostException`, `SocketTimeoutException`) usually means no complete response arrived: offline, DNS failure or timeout
`HttpException` means the server replied with a non-2xx status, and `e.code()` tells 401 from 404 from 503
Mapping these to a domain error type in the repository keeps Retrofit/OkHttp types out of the UI layer
A blanket `catch (e: Exception)` that turns everything into an error state is fine inside `viewModelScope.launch`
A `SerializationException` means the device is offline
questions.explanation: Transport failures surface as `IOException` and server error statuses as `HttpException`, and the repository should translate both into domain errors. A blanket `catch (e: Exception)` also swallows `CancellationException`, which breaks cancellation, so rethrow it. A `SerializationException` means the payload didn't match the model, not that the device is offline.

questions.question: The `OkHttpClient` has a `Cache(File(context.cacheDir, "http"), 10L * 1024 * 1024)`. A GET response came back with `Cache-Control: max-age=60`. The user repeats the same GET 30 seconds later. What happens?
options: OkHttp serves the stored response from disk with no network request
OkHttp always sends a conditional request with `If-None-Match` first
It goes to the network, because Retrofit bypasses OkHttp's cache
Nothing is cached, because only POST responses are cacheable
questions.explanation: The response is still fresh (30 s < 60 s), so the cache answers on its own. Conditional requests (`If-None-Match`/`If-Modified-Since`) happen only once the entry is stale and has validators. Retrofit runs on OkHttp, so the cache applies to its calls.

questions.question: It is safe to add a generic retry-with-backoff interceptor that retries every request, including `POST /payments`, after a `SocketTimeoutException`.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A timeout doesn't tell you whether the server processed the request, so retrying a non-idempotent POST can charge the user twice. Automatically retry only idempotent requests (GET, PUT, DELETE), or send an idempotency key that the server deduplicates.

questions.question: The app sends a PATCH body built with a default `Json` instance. What JSON does `Json.encodeToString(Patch(name = "A"))` produce?
options: {"display_name":"A"}
{"display_name":"A","bio":null}
{"name":"A"}
{"name":"A","bio":null}
questions.explanation: `@SerialName` renames the key. `encodeDefaults` is false by default, so `bio`, which still equals its default `null`, is left out. A server that expects an explicit `null` to clear a field never receives one. Turn on `encodeDefaults = true` (or use `@EncodeDefault`) when that matters.

questions.question: Which statements about OkHttp application interceptors (`addInterceptor`) and network interceptors (`addNetworkInterceptor`) are true?
options: An application interceptor runs once per call, even when OkHttp follows a redirect or retries
A network interceptor runs for every network request, including each redirect hop
An application interceptor can return a response without calling `chain.proceed()`
An application interceptor sees the `Accept-Encoding: gzip` header that OkHttp adds transparently
A network interceptor runs even when the response comes entirely from the cache
questions.explanation: Application interceptors wrap the whole call: they run once, see the request as your code built it, and can short-circuit it. Network interceptors sit next to the wire, so they run on every hop and see headers OkHttp adds such as `Accept-Encoding`. A pure cache hit never reaches them.

questions.question: Five parallel requests all get 401 because the access token expired. Which `Authenticator.authenticate()` strategy is correct?
options: Synchronize, reuse a token another call already refreshed, else refresh once; return `null` on failure or repeat
Each call refreshes the token on its own and retries, so all five recover independently and in parallel
Return `response.request` unchanged so OkHttp retries it, since the server may have refreshed the session
Throw an `IOException` so Retrofit retries the call automatically after a backoff
questions.explanation: Without synchronization, five 401s cause five refreshes, which can invalidate each other's refresh tokens. Comparing tokens lets the waiting calls reuse the new token. Returning `null` (also after a retry, detectable via `priorResponse`) stops the loop, whereas returning the unchanged request just repeats the 401 until OkHttp gives up on too many follow-ups.

questions.question: What is the main operational risk of adding certificate pinning (OkHttp `CertificatePinner` or a network security config `pin-set`)?
options: If the server key rotates outside the pin set, installed versions can't connect until users update
It turns off TLS hostname verification for the pinned host, since the pin already identifies the server
It makes HTTPS unnecessary, so cleartext gets allowed for that host
It cannot be bypassed even on rooted devices, so debugging proxies stop working permanently
questions.explanation: Pinning narrows which certificates are trusted, so an unplanned key or CA change locks out every old build. Mitigate with backup pins (SPKI hashes of a spare key or intermediate) and a `pin-set` expiration. Pinning adds to normal TLS checks rather than replacing them, and it can be bypassed on rooted devices.
